Clean plexus map

Roots, trunks, divisions

Roots

  • Anterior rami of C5–C8 and most of T1
  • Receive gray rami communicantes (sympathetic fibres) near origin
  • Pass through posterior triangle, between anterior and middle scalene
  • Lie superior and posterior to subclavian artery
  • Branches: dorsal scapular (C5) → rhomboids; long thoracic (C5–C7) → serratus anterior

Trunks

  • Superior: C5 + C6
  • Middle: continuation of C7
  • Inferior: C8 + T1
  • Pass laterally over rib I, enter axilla
  • Inferior trunk lies on rib I, posterior to subclavian artery
  • Only branches (from upper trunk): suprascapular nerve + nerve to subclavius (both C5–C6)
  • Upper trunk = Erb’s point: formed by 2 nerves, ends as 2 nerves, has 2 branches

Divisions

  • Each trunk → 1 anterior + 1 posterior division (3 + 3 = 6)
  • Anterior → nerves of anterior compartments of arm and forearm
  • Posterior → nerves of posterior compartments
  • No peripheral nerves come directly from divisions

Rule of thumb

  • Anterior compartment nerves ← medial and lateral cords
  • Posterior compartment nerves ← posterior cord
  • Cords relate to the 2nd part of the axillary artery

Cords and their branches

Lateral cord

  • Anterior divisions of upper + middle trunks (C5–C7)
  • Lateral to axillary artery
  • 3 nerves: lateral pectoral · musculocutaneous · lateral root of median

Medial cord

  • Continuation of anterior division of inferior trunk (C8, T1)
  • Medial to axillary artery
  • 5 branches: medial pectoral · medial cutaneous n. of arm · medial cutaneous n. of forearm · medial root of median · ulnar

Posterior cord

  • Union of all 3 posterior divisions (C5–T1)
  • Posterior to axillary artery
  • 5 nerves: superior subscapular · thoracodorsal · inferior subscapular · axillary · radial

“M” sign

  • Musculocutaneous, lateral root, median, medial root and ulnar form an M over the 3rd part of the axillary artery

Clinical

Erb’s paralysis

  • Superior trunk: C5, C6 roots, suprascapular n., nerve to subclavius, anterior + posterior divisions
  • “Waiter’s tip”: arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated

Klumpke’s paralysis

  • Inferior trunk: C8, T1 roots
  • Claw hand: hyperextension at MCP, flexion at IP joints
  • May go with Horner’s syndrome
Where injury hits: cervical spinal cord injury or pulling → roots · severe trauma to 1st rib → trunks · glenohumeral dislocation → divisions and cords

Check on your drawing

  • Lower subscapular nerve supplies teres major too (Table 2.5). Your drawing only lists subscapularis.
  • “Median pectoral” and “median brachial/antebrachial cutaneous” should be medial. Median is a different nerve.
  • The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm supplies skin of the medial arm and the axilla floor. Forearm skin (medial and posterior) belongs to the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm. Your brachial label has forearm skin mixed in.
  • Everything else (roots, trunks, cords, M-sign branches) matches the book.

Myotomes and dermatomes

Movements

  • Shoulder abduction: C5
  • Elbow flexion: C6 (C5)
  • Elbow extension: C7
  • Finger flexion: C8
  • Finger abduction/adduction: T1

Reflexes and skin

  • Biceps tendon tap: C6
  • Triceps tendon tap: C7
  • Skin: C5 upper lateral arm · C6 thumb pad · C7 index pad · C8 little finger pad · T1 medial elbow
Peripheral nerve injury = loss of sensation in that nerve’s area. Spinal nerve injury = loss in a dermatome.

Who supplies what

  • Musculocutaneous: anterior arm; skin of anterolateral forearm
  • Median: anterior forearm except FCU + medial half of FDP; thenar muscles + 2 lateral lumbricals; palmar lateral 3½ digits
  • Ulnar: FCU, medial half FDP; most intrinsic hand muscles; medial 1½ digits
  • Radial: all posterior arm and forearm muscles; skin of posterior forearm and dorsolateral hand

Course of the big three

Median (C5–T1)

  • Crosses brachial artery lateral to medial → most medial content of cubital fossa
  • Between 2 heads of pronator teres → between FDS and FDP → between palmaris longus and FCR tendons → carpal tunnel
  • Anterior interosseous nerve: FPL, lateral half FDP, pronator quadratus
  • Palmar branch passes over the retinaculum, so it is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome

Ulnar (C7–T1)

  • Pierces medial intermuscular septum → behind medial epicondyle → between 2 heads of FCU
  • Forearm: only FCU + medial half FDP
  • Enters hand superficial to retinaculum, through Guyon’s canal, lateral to pisiform
  • Deep branch (motor): hypothenar, interossei, adductor pollicis, 2 medial lumbricals. Superficial branch (sensory): palmaris brevis + little finger and medial half of ring finger

Radial (C5–T1)

  • Through triangular interval → spiral groove → pierces lateral intermuscular septum
  • Supplies triceps, anconeus; brachioradialis + ECRL before dividing
  • Superficial branch: sensory. Deep branch: motor, through supinator, becomes posterior interosseous nerve

Nerves and bone

Surgical neck → axillary nerve
Radial groove → radial nerve
Medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve

More clinical points

  • Anterior interosseous palsy: weak FPL + lateral FDP + pronator quadratus. Can’t make the “OK” sign
  • Pronator teres syndrome: median entrapment between the 2 heads or by ligament of Struthers
  • Cubital tunnel syndrome: ulnar entrapment between 2 heads of FCU
  • Wartenberg’s syndrome: superficial radial entrapment between brachioradialis and ECRL
  • Ulnar injury (elbow or wrist): claw hand, MCP hyperextended, IP flexed, adductor pollicis lost. Claw is worse at the wrist, because at the elbow the medial FDP is paralysed too
  • Dorsal branch of ulnar nerve (leaves in distal forearm): intact dorsal hand sensation → lesion at the wrist; lost → lesion more proximal

Spaces

Quadrangular

Teres minor, teres major, long head triceps, surgical neck. Axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral vessels

Triangular interval

Long head triceps, humerus shaft, teres major. Radial nerve + profunda brachii

Rotator cuff = SITS: Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. Axillary n. = deltoid + teres minor. Suprascapular = supra + infraspinatus.

More important points

Page 80 (axilla and breast)

  • Pectoralis major forms most of the anterior axillary wall and attaches humerus to chest wall
  • The breast lies over it; the axillary process extends round its lateral margin into the axilla
  • Lymph from the lateral and superior breast drains mainly to axillary nodes

Hand nerves (page 219–221)

  • Ulnar, median and radial all give skin supply; radial only supplies the dorsolateral hand
  • Ulnar divides just distal to the pisiform into deep (motor) and superficial (sensory) branches
  • Deep branch runs through Guyon’s canal between the hook of hamate and flexor tendons; ganglia can compress it
  • Ulnar injury sites: behind the medial epicondyle and at the wrist (lateral to pisiform)
  • Palm incisions: parallel to creases, longer than dorsal ones, cross flexion creases in a Z shape
Radial nerve (page 194): it supplies brachioradialis + ECRL before dividing. Deep branch supplies ECRB, passes through supinator, supplies it, then emerges as the posterior interosseous nerve for the remaining extensors.

Remember

  • Roots 5 (C5–T1) · Trunks 3 · Divisions 6 · Cords 3
  • Lateral = 3 nerves · Medial = 5 · Posterior = 5
  • Only trunk branches: suprascapular + nerve to subclavius (upper trunk)
  • Upper trunk → Erb’s · Lower trunk → Klumpke’s
